Unofficial integration, not affiliated with Legrand. It turns on and off the lights of a Legrand In One (powerline, "CPL") installation from Gladys, and shows their state when someone presses a wall switch.

## What you need

- A Legrand USB / RS232 interface, reference 882 13, plugged into the machine that runs Gladys.
- A small "serial gateway" container that exposes this USB device on a TCP port. Gladys integrations cannot access USB devices directly, so this container does it for them (see the project README for a ready-to-use `docker-compose.yml`).

## Setup

1. Start the serial gateway container. By default it listens on `172.17.0.1:2000`.
2. Install this integration and check the address and port in its settings.
3. **Press each wall switch once.** The Legrand bus cannot list its devices, so the integration learns each circuit from the frames the switches send when they are pressed.
4. Open the Discovery tab and run a scan. Each circuit seen on the bus appears as a light named `Legrand <id>-<unit>`, followed in brackets by the kind of device: `(inter)` for a switch, `(inter scenario)` for the on/off key of a scenario switch. This is deduced from the keys heard so far: a scenario switch whose on/off key alone was pressed first shows as `(inter)`, then turns to `(inter scenario)` once one of its scene keys is heard. Create the circuits you want and rename them.

If a switch does not appear, press it again and rescan. The list of known circuits is kept across restarts.

## What it does

- Turns lights on and off from Gladys (dashboard, scenes, voice).
- Updates the state in Gladys when a wall switch is used.
- Shows each Legrand scenario button as a button in Gladys (`Legrand scenario <id>-<unit>`). It clicks when the scenario is pressed, so you can use it as a trigger in Gladys scenes.

## Linked devices

The bus never reports the state of a receiver. When a button drives several lights (a group, a scenario), only the button sends a frame and the lights stay silent. The settings **Rule 1** to **Rule 12** (one rule per field) tell the integration which lights follow which button. Nothing is sent on the bus: only the state shown in Gladys is updated.

Use the circuit numbers printed in the logs (`944559-1`). One rule per field. If you need more than 12 rules, put several in one field, separated by `;`:

```
648966-1 -> 944559-1, 944559-2
648966-2 -> 944559-1=on, 944559-2=off
```

Several rules in one field: `929520-1 -> 944561-1; 929523-1 -> 944561-1`.

- With a light on the left, the lights on the right copy its state (on, off), whether it comes from a wall switch or from a command in Gladys.
- With a scenario button on the left, each light on the right takes the fixed state written after `=` (`on` or `off`).

## Tested hardware

This integration was developed on one installation, with:

- the Legrand PLC/USB interface **ref. 882 13** (seen by Linux as a BTicino "SFERA Tele Loop" USB serial device);
- double transmitter-receiver switches **ref. 672 02** (two directions: top key = on, bottom key = off);
- a single transmitter-receiver switch **ref. 672 01** (frames received and decoded; command from Gladys not tested);
- a lighting scenario switch **ref. 672 08** (on/off keys + two scenario keys);
- a scenario transmitter **ref. 672 80** (four scenario keys);
- Gladys Assistant 5.3 on a Home Assistant Yellow (64-bit ARM).

## How to read the devices in Gladys

In the In One system every product has a unique identifier, and every receiver *learns* the transmitters that drive it (LEARN key). Only **transmitter** orders travel on the bus: "direction 1 of transmitter 944559 says *on*". The receivers that learned this transmitter react, silently.

So a device `Legrand 944559-1` in Gladys is **a transmitter key** (identifier 944559, direction 1), not a lamp. Driving it from Gladys is like pressing that key: every receiver that learned it reacts. This is why a transmitter learned by several receivers switches several lamps, and why the state of a receiver can never be read: it does not exist on the bus. The **Linked devices** setting describes these associations so that Gladys shows the right state.

## References of the In One PLC range

From the Céliane technical guide. Only the four references above were tested; for the others the "Expected" column says what the protocol suggests, **without verification**.

**Lighting**

| Reference | Product | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| 672 01 | Single transmitter-receiver switch 2,500 W | **Tested** for reception; command expected to work like the 672 02 |
| 672 02 | Double transmitter-receiver switch 2 × 1,000 W | **Tested** |
| 672 03 / 672 04 | Single / double switch with indicator | Like 672 01 / 672 02: should work (the indicator is local, nothing on the bus) |
| 672 08 | Lighting scenario switch (on/off + 2 scenarios) | **Tested** |
| 672 15 | Automatic switch 1,000 W (motion detector) | Should send on/off orders like a switch |
| 672 10 / 672 12 / 672 14, 036 10 | Dimmers 300 W, 600 W and DIN dimmer 1,000 W | On/off only; no level control in this version |
| 882 03 | Plug-in dimmer 500 W | On/off only |
| 882 00, 882 01, 882 15, 882 20 | Infrared/radio remotes and scenario controls | No: they do not use the PLC bus, except through a PLC/IR receiver that relays |

**Scenarios**

| Reference | Product | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| 672 80 | Scenario transmitter (4 scenarios) | **Tested** |
| 672 84 | Touch-screen scenario manager | Its scenarios should show up as buttons; not verified |

**Roller shutters and blinds**

| Reference | Product | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| 672 51 / 672 55 / 672 56 | Individual shutter switch (plain, with override, with programmable level) | Not supported in this version (up/down/stop orders, another family of the protocol) |
| 672 53 / 672 54 | Central control / group control (4 zones) | Not supported in this version |

**Heating, detectors, interfaces**: thermostats 674 40 / 674 42, cable outlet 674 45, local override 674 48, programmer 674 49, detectors 675 22 / 675 23 / 675 24, interfaces 036 06 / 036 07 / 036 18 — outside the scope of this integration. Filters 882 12 / 882 21 / 882 23 are passive accessories.

If you test one of these references, say so on the project's GitHub repository: the table will be updated.

## Limits of this version

- The bus never reports the real state of a receiver. The state shown in Gladys is deduced from the frames and from the commands sent, so it can drift (for example after a Legrand scenario that switches lights off). A command from Gladys always puts it back in line.
- To keep Gladys up to date after a Legrand scenario, use linked devices (rule `scenario -> light=on`).
- On/off lights only: no dimmers, no shutters, and Gladys cannot start a Legrand scenario.

## Cómo instalar Legrand In One CPL en Gladys

1. En Gladys, abre **Integraciones**: Legrand In One CPL aparece en el catálogo junto a las integraciones nativas, con una insignia de comunidad.
2. Haz clic en **Instalar**. Gladys descarga la imagen Docker (`ghcr.io/xdeco/gladys-integration-legrand-inone:0.4.0`), la ejecuta en un entorno aislado del núcleo y genera la interfaz de la integración (dispositivos, descubrimiento y configuración).
3. Abre la pantalla de **Configuración** de la integración, rellena los parámetros y guarda.
4. También puedes instalarla directamente desde la URL de su repositorio: [https://github.com/XDECO/gladys-integration-legrand-inone](https://github.com/XDECO/gladys-integration-legrand-inone).

Legrand In One CPL requiere Gladys `>=4.86.0`. El catálogo de Gladys se actualiza cada hora, así que una nueva versión está disponible como máximo una hora después de publicarse.

¿Todavía no usas Gladys? Es gratuito y de código abierto: [sigue la guía de instalación](/es/docs/) para empezar.

## Sobre las integraciones externas

Legrand In One CPL es una **integración externa**: una integración comunitaria empaquetada como contenedor Docker y publicada en GitHub. Gladys la instala con un clic y la ejecuta en un entorno aislado del núcleo. La publica y mantiene [XDECO](https://github.com/XDECO), no el equipo principal de Gladys.
